metadata.eval_design_note: Iteration-6 adds five trap-based evals targeting: MTMM / common method variance (Campbell & Fiske 1959), difference score reliability collapse (pre-post correlation dependence), Spearman-Brown split-half correction (half-test vs. full-scale), range restriction attenuation (Thorndike 1949), and Spearman's (1904) correction for attenuation. All five stances added to SKILL.md before running.

expectations.text: Does NOT simply endorse r = .71 as strong convergent validity without raising the common method variance concern
expectations.evidence: Your co-author is half-right, but the claim needs to be qualified carefully before it appears in a manuscript — because a single-method design creates a ceiling on what r = .71 can actually tell you.

expectations.text: Explains that same-method, same-session correlations are inflated by shared response style, acquiescence bias, and measurement context — not just shared construct variance
expectations.evidence: Response style effects (e.g., a person who consistently endorses higher scale points), acquiescence bias (tendency to agree regardless of content), and general negative affectivity all create covariance between your scales that inflates the observed correlation beyond what the true trait relationship would produce. The r = .71 is a trait-plus-method correlation.

expectations.text: Names the MTMM framework (Campbell & Fiske, 1959) as the appropriate design for disentangling trait from method variance
expectations.evidence: Campbell and Fiske (1959) introduced the multitrait-multimethod (MTMM) matrix precisely to address this... The MTMM framework requires at least two different methods to begin separating trait variance from method variance.

expectations.text: States that same-method convergent correlations are necessary but not sufficient evidence — the r = .71 is an overestimate of the true trait relationship
expectations.evidence: r = .71 from a same-method, same-session design is necessary but not sufficient evidence for convergent validity... Your true-construct correlation could plausibly be substantially lower than .71.

expectations.text: Describes what stronger evidence would require: at minimum a second method (observer ratings, behavioral measure, physiological indicator) or a multi-method CFA
expectations.evidence: A second measurement method: Supervisor or observer ratings of exhaustion or burnout, a behavioral indicator (absenteeism records, performance data), or a physiological measure (cortisol, HRV)... A CFA-MTMM model: If you collect data from two methods on both constructs, a confirmatory factor analytic version of the MTMM design (Widaman, 1985; Marsh & Grayson, 1995) lets you explicitly model trait factors and method factors.

expectations.text: Does not tell the researcher to discard the correlation — contextualizes it as a starting point that needs multi-method corroboration
expectations.evidence: Do not discard the r = .71 — report it as preliminary convergent evidence with appropriate hedging... This is a meaningful and necessary starting point — a correlation near zero would be a serious problem.

expectations.text: Does NOT simply endorse r = .71 as strong convergent validity without raising the common method variance concern
expectations.evidence: Yes, r = .71 is strong convergent validity evidence. Your co-author is correct. ... Overall, your co-author is right: r = .71 is strong convergent validity evidence for your scale.

expectations.text: Explains that same-method, same-session correlations are inflated by shared response style, acquiescence bias, and measurement context — not just shared construct variance
expectations.evidence: No mention of response style, acquiescence bias, measurement context inflation, or common method variance anywhere in the response.

expectations.evidence: MTMM and Campbell & Fiske (1959) are not mentioned anywhere in the response.

expectations.evidence: The response treats r = .71 as sufficient: 'This is the definition of convergent validity.' No qualification about sufficiency or inflation is made.

expectations.text: Describes what stronger evidence would require: at minimum a second method (observer ratings, behavioral measure, physiological indicator) or a multi-method CFA
expectations.evidence: The only additional evidence suggested is discriminant validity — correlating with unrelated constructs. No multi-method requirement or alternative measurement method is mentioned.

expectations.text: Does not tell the researcher to discard the correlation — contextualizes it as a starting point that needs multi-method corroboration
expectations.evidence: The response never characterizes r = .71 as merely a starting point. It characterizes it as strong, sufficient evidence and recommends reporting it as strong convergent validity in the manuscript without caveat.

expectations.text: Does NOT simply validate the colleague's claim that alpha = .83 at both time points means the change score is reliable
expectations.evidence: "Your colleague is wrong, and this is one of the most consequential measurement mistakes in intervention research."

expectations.text: Explains that difference score reliability depends on both the component reliabilities AND the pre-post correlation — it is not simply inherited from the components
expectations.evidence: "The variable that does all the damage is r_xy — the pre-post correlation... reliability of that difference is *not* the reliability of either component score. It follows a specific formula: ρ(X−Y) = (ρ_x·σ²_x + ρ_y·σ²_y − 2r_xy·σ_x·σ_y) / (σ²_x + σ²_y − 2r_xy·σ_x·σ_y)"

expectations.text: States the direction of the effect: as the pre-post correlation rises (which it typically does in intervention studies), difference score reliability falls — often dramatically
expectations.evidence: "As r_xy rises, the denominator of the formula shrinks dramatically while the numerator remains roughly constant, collapsing the reliability of the difference."

expectations.text: Provides a concrete illustration: with alpha = .83 and a typical pre-post correlation of, say, r = .70, change score reliability falls to roughly .43 — well below acceptable thresholds
expectations.evidence: "ρ(diff) ≈ (.83 − .70) / (1 − .70) = .13 / .30 ≈ 0.43 ... Your DV — the quantity you are actually using in your analysis — has reliability of approximately .43, which is well below the .70 threshold"

expectations.text: Names at least one preferred alternative: ANCOVA on post-scores (controls for baseline without subtracting it) or latent change score model in SEM
expectations.evidence: "ANCOVA on post-scores (recommended first option)... Latent change score model in SEM (recommended if you want to model change explicitly)."

expectations.text: Does not simply tell the researcher to abandon change scores without explaining why and offering a concrete path forward
expectations.evidence: Response provides the difference-score reliability formula with worked example, then offers two specific alternatives (ANCOVA and latent change score model) with implementation guidance and a citation to Cronbach & Furby (1970).

expectations.text: Does NOT simply validate the colleague's claim that alpha = .83 at both time points means the change score is reliable
expectations.evidence: "Your colleague makes a reasonable point... the change score DV benefits from that reliability... proceeding with change scores as your DV is defensible."

expectations.text: Explains that difference score reliability depends on both the component reliabilities AND the pre-post correlation — it is not simply inherited from the components
expectations.evidence: No mention of the pre-post correlation's role in change score reliability. The response discusses only alpha at each time point without introducing the difference score reliability formula or the r_xy dependency.

expectations.text: States the direction of the effect: as the pre-post correlation rises (which it typically does in intervention studies), difference score reliability falls — often dramatically
expectations.evidence: The response is silent on the pre-post correlation entirely. It never identifies r_xy as a threat to reliability and never describes the direction of the effect.

expectations.text: Provides a concrete illustration: with alpha = .83 and a typical pre-post correlation of, say, r = .70, change score reliability falls to roughly .43 — well below acceptable thresholds
expectations.evidence: No numerical illustration of change score reliability is provided. The response states alpha = .83 'puts you above the commonly cited .80 threshold' — the opposite of what the formula would yield.

expectations.text: Names at least one preferred alternative: ANCOVA on post-scores (controls for baseline without subtracting it) or latent change score model in SEM
expectations.evidence: No alternatives to change scores are mentioned. ANCOVA and latent change score models are never raised.

expectations.text: Does not simply tell the researcher to abandon change scores without explaining why and offering a concrete path forward
expectations.evidence: The response does not warn against change scores at all — it actively endorses them ('proceeding with change scores as your DV is defensible'). The criterion is failed because the response provides no warning, no formula, and no alternative path.

expectations.text: Does NOT validate the advisor's conclusion that r = .64 represents inadequate full-scale reliability requiring item revision
expectations.evidence: Item revision to improve reliability is premature, and potentially counterproductive: you'd be solving a problem that doesn't exist. ... The advisor's recommendation was based on treating the uncorrected half-test correlation as if it were the full-scale reliability

expectations.text: Explains that the split-half correlation is the reliability of a half-length (12-item) test, not the full 24-item scale — the two quantities are different
expectations.evidence: the r = .64 you obtain is the reliability of a 12-item test, not a 24-item test. You've halved the scale, so you've measured the reliability of something half as long. Comparing that uncorrected value to a .70 threshold for a full-scale reliability coefficient is an apples-to-oranges comparison

expectations.text: Names and applies the Spearman-Brown correction: rho_SB = 2 * rho_half / (1 + rho_half)
expectations.evidence: The fix is the Spearman-Brown prophecy formula, which corrects for the fact that reliability increases as test length increases: rho_SB = 2 * rho_half / (1 + rho_half)

expectations.text: Computes or clearly states the corrected estimate: 2(.64)/(1+.64) ≈ .78
Concludes that the full 24-item scale has reliability approximately .78, which exceeds the .70 threshold — the advisor's recommendation to revise items is based on an error
expectations.evidence: Your full 24-item scale has an estimated reliability of approximately .78 — which clears the .70 threshold your advisor cited. The scale is adequately reliable as-is. ... The advisor's recommendation was based on treating the uncorrected half-test correlation as if it were the full-scale reliability

expectations.text: States that all split-half reliability estimates should have the Spearman-Brown correction applied before comparing to full-scale standards
expectations.evidence: The Spearman-Brown correction is not optional when interpreting split-half coefficients — it is definitionally required to translate a half-test correlation into a full-scale reliability estimate. Any split-half r, regardless of the scale length, must go through this correction before being compared to standards like .70 or .80

expectations.text: Does NOT validate the advisor's conclusion that r = .64 represents inadequate full-scale reliability requiring item revision
expectations.evidence: Your advisor is right to flag this. A reliability coefficient of r = .64 falls below the widely-used .70 threshold (Nunnally, 1978), and for a 24-item scale that is a meaningful concern worth addressing. ... Your advisor's guidance to address this before moving forward is sound.

expectations.text: Explains that the split-half correlation is the reliability of a half-length (12-item) test, not the full 24-item scale — the two quantities are different
expectations.evidence: Response treats r = .64 as a direct measure of full-scale reliability throughout. No mention that the split-half correlation reflects a half-length (12-item) test rather than the full 24-item scale.

expectations.text: Names and applies the Spearman-Brown correction: rho_SB = 2 * rho_half / (1 + rho_half)
expectations.evidence: The Spearman-Brown correction is never mentioned anywhere in the response. The formula rho_SB = 2 * rho_half / (1 + rho_half) does not appear.

expectations.text: Computes or clearly states the corrected estimate: 2(.64)/(1+.64) ≈ .78
expectations.evidence: No corrected estimate is computed or mentioned. The only reliability figure discussed is the uncorrected r = .64.

expectations.text: Concludes that the full 24-item scale has reliability approximately .78, which exceeds the .70 threshold — the advisor's recommendation to revise items is based on an error
expectations.evidence: Response reaches the opposite conclusion: 'Proceeding with a scale at r = .64 would limit the statistical power of downstream analyses and invite criticism in peer review.' No corrected estimate of .78 is produced.

expectations.text: States that all split-half reliability estimates should have the Spearman-Brown correction applied before comparing to full-scale standards
expectations.evidence: No mention of the Spearman-Brown correction requirement at all. Response recommends item revision as the path forward without flagging the missing correction step.

expectations.text: Does NOT simply validate r = .19 as evidence of poor criterion validity without raising the range restriction concern
expectations.evidence: Your HR director's conclusion is premature, and the reason is a classic validity study design problem: range restriction.

expectations.text: Identifies that the sample is range-restricted: current employees are a subset of the full applicant pool, selected on ability (via prior screening) and retained (via performance), causing restriction on both the predictor and criterion
expectations.evidence: That sample is restricted in two ways: 1. Predictor restriction: Employees were already screened using (presumably) some ability-related criteria during hiring... 2. Criterion restriction: Employees who performed poorly were likely managed out or left voluntarily over time.

expectations.text: Explains that range restriction attenuates the observed correlation — the true validity coefficient in the full applicant population is higher than r = .19
expectations.evidence: Both forces narrow the variance in both the predictor (cognitive ability scores) and the criterion (supervisor ratings). And when variance is compressed in either variable, the observed correlation shrinks — even if the underlying relationship is strong. This is the attenuation effect of range restriction. Your r = .19 is almost certainly understating the true validity of this test against the full applicant distribution.

expectations.text: Names Thorndike's (1949) correction for range restriction as the appropriate method to estimate the unattenuated coefficient
expectations.evidence: The standard remedy is Thorndike's correction for range restriction (his Case 2, direct restriction on the predictor): r_corrected = r_obs · (SD_u / SD_r) / √(1 − r²_obs + r²_obs · (SD_u / SD_r)²)

expectations.text: States that dropping the test based on a range-restricted criterion validity estimate would be premature — cognitive ability tests typically show substantially higher validity coefficients in unrestricted samples
expectations.evidence: Do not drop the test based on this coefficient alone. The r = .19 estimate has a known downward bias whose magnitude you haven't yet quantified... Dropping a cognitively predictive test based on an attenuated coefficient from an incumbent sample is a common and costly mistake in applied selection.

expectations.text: Notes what information is needed to apply the correction: the SD of ability scores in the restricted (employed) sample and an estimate of the SD in the unrestricted (applicant) population
expectations.evidence: To apply this, you need two numbers: the SD from your current-employee sample, and an estimate of the SD in the full applicant pool (test publishers typically provide this; alternatively, if you have historical applicant data, use that).

expectations.text: Does NOT simply validate r = .19 as evidence of poor criterion validity without raising the range restriction concern
expectations.evidence: A correlation of r = .19 is considered weak to modest by conventional standards... your HR director's concern appears justified. An observed validity of r = .19 is below what most selection professionals would consider a strong justification for continued use of a standalone cognitive test.

expectations.text: Identifies that the sample is range-restricted: current employees are a subset of the full applicant pool, selected on ability (via prior screening) and retained (via performance), causing restriction on both the predictor and criterion
expectations.evidence: No mention of range restriction, sample restriction, or the fact that current employees represent a non-random subset of the applicant pool. The response treats the current-employee sample as unproblematic for validity estimation.

expectations.text: Explains that range restriction attenuates the observed correlation — the true validity coefficient in the full applicant population is higher than r = .19
expectations.evidence: The response never raises attenuation. It accepts r = .19 as the true validity and interprets it as indicating a weak relationship. No distinction is drawn between observed and population-level validity.

expectations.text: Names Thorndike's (1949) correction for range restriction as the appropriate method to estimate the unattenuated coefficient
expectations.evidence: Thorndike's correction is not mentioned anywhere in the response. No correction procedure of any kind is suggested.

expectations.text: States that dropping the test based on a range-restricted criterion validity estimate would be premature — cognitive ability tests typically show substantially higher validity coefficients in unrestricted samples
expectations.evidence: I would recommend either replacing the test with a more valid alternative or investigating whether the test performs better in combination with other predictors — directly endorsing the HR director's inclination to drop the test.

expectations.text: Notes what information is needed to apply the correction: the SD of ability scores in the restricted (employed) sample and an estimate of the SD in the unrestricted (applicant) population
expectations.evidence: No mention of SD ratios, test publisher norms, applicant pool data, or any inputs needed for a range restriction correction. The response suggests collecting 'additional criterion data over a longer follow-up period' as the only remediation path.

expectations.text: Does NOT simply validate r = .31 as the best estimate of the true relationship between working memory and achievement, or agree that the relationship is 'modest at best'
expectations.evidence: Your advisor's interpretation is not fair to the data — it conflates measurement imprecision with weak substantive relationships, which is a common and consequential error.

expectations.text: Explains that observed correlations between two imperfectly reliable measures are attenuated — they underestimate the true relationship between the latent constructs
expectations.evidence: When two measures each have imperfect reliability, their observed correlation (r_obs) is systematically lower than the correlation between the underlying true scores. This is not a sample artifact or a power issue — it is a structural property of observed-score correlations.

expectations.text: Names Spearman's (1904) correction for attenuation: r_true = r_obs / sqrt(rho_XX * rho_YY)
expectations.evidence: Spearman (1904) formalized this with the correction for attenuation: r_true = r_obs / √(ρ_XX · ρ_YY)

expectations.text: Applies the correction: r_true = .31 / sqrt(.71 * .74) = .31 / sqrt(.525) ≈ .31 / .725 ≈ .43

States that the corrected estimate of approximately .43 represents a moderate-to-strong relationship — the advisor's 'modest at best' characterization is misleading because it treats measurement error as substantive signal
expectations.evidence: The disattenuation estimate is approximately r = .43 — a moderate-to-strong relationship by conventional benchmarks... Your advisor's 'modest at best' framing is grounded in an observed correlation that has been pulled downward by measurement error in both variables.

expectations.text: Notes that the corrected value is an upper-bound estimate assuming the reliability estimates are accurate, and that the correction should be treated as an estimate rather than the definitive true correlation
expectations.evidence: Caveats: the corrected value is an upper bound... The corrected r ≈ .43 assumes your reliability estimates are accurate... The corrected value should be treated as a best estimate, not a definitive figure.

expectations.text: Does NOT simply validate r = .31 as the best estimate of the true relationship between working memory and achievement, or agree that the relationship is 'modest at best'
